html:
Kush was an ancient kingdom in Nubia, along the Nile in what is now northern Sudan, that ruled from about 1070 BCE to the 4th century CE. For about a century it ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty, and later flourished from its southern capital at Meroë.

It rose in the same lands as Kerma, the older Nubian kingdom that Egypt had crushed. After centuries of Egyptian rule during the New Kingdom, Nubia broke free when Egypt weakened, and a new kingdom took shape around Napata, at the foot of the sacred mountain Jebel Barkal. Its kings worshipped Amun and used Egyptian titles and writing, but kept a distinct Kushite identity.

Its main phases:

  • The 25th Dynasty, about 747 to 656 BCE. King Piye marched north and conquered Egypt. His successors, above all Taharqa, ruled from Nubia to the Mediterranean and built across both lands. The Assyrians drove them out of Egypt by 656 BCE.
  • Napata. The kings kept ruling Nubia from Napata, and were buried under steep pyramids.
  • Meroë. From about the 3rd century BCE the centre moved south to Meroë, on the savanna, where rain-fed farming and cattle supported a large city.

Meroë was a centre of iron smelting, with slag heaps still visible. Its people wrote their own language in the Meroitic script, which can be read aloud but is still not understood. Nubia has more than two hundred pyramids, most of them at Meroë, more than all of Egypt. Queens called Kandake held real power; one negotiated with the Roman Empire after a war in the 20s BCE.

Kush declined in the 3rd and 4th centuries as trade shifted to the Red Sea, and around 350 CE an army of Aksum raided its lands. Christian Nubian kingdoms later rose on its ruins.
